tier_reason: README Performance table compares jaq-3.0 with jq-1.8.1 and gojq-0.12.18 on 30 filters; the harness is public (bench.sh plus examples/benches.json and examples/benches/*.jq, timed with /usr/bin/time -f %U, min of 3 runs for the 27 filter rows), the build is cargo build --release with the public Cargo.toml release profile (codegen-units = 1, strip), jq comes from the Arch Linux package and the CPU is named (AMD Ryzen 5 5500U). rustc version is not stated, which matches earlier wave-12 A entries that use distro-package baselines.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (ms, user CPU time): jaq-3.0 is fastest of the three on 20 of 30 benchmarks, jq-1.8.1 on 5, gojq-0.12.18 on 6. Against jq: sort 90 vs 430, group-by 260 vs 1790, to-fromjson 50 vs 350, tree-contains 90 vs 830, bf-fib 530 vs 1030, reverse 30 vs 440, kv-update 130 vs 440, str-slice 170 vs 650; upto and reduce-update round to 0 ms for jaq vs 440 and 720 ms for jq; startup ('empty' x512) 410 vs 430. jq is faster on reduce (700 vs 740), try-catch (200 vs 220), pyramid (250 vs 300), tree-flatten (330 vs 700), ack (490 vs 570), range-prop (250 vs 370) and cumsum-xy (350 vs 380). Head to head with jq, jaq is faster on 23 of 30 rows and slower on 7 (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: jaq: cargo build --release with the workspace release profile (codegen-units = 1, strip = true); rustc version not stated. jq-1.8.1 from the official Arch Linux package; gojq-0.12.18 GitHub release binary. Timing: bench.sh with 'timeout 10 /usr/bin/time -f %U' (user CPU seconds), min of 3 runs per filter row (single run for empty, bf-fib and defs); filter outputs are piped through '| length' and discarded.
corrections.caveats: Author-run benchmarks on one laptop CPU; times are user CPU time, not wall time (system time and, for gojq, multi-threaded GC accounting differ). jq is a distro build whose flags are not restated. jaq loses to jq on 7 of 30 rows (reduce, try-catch, pyramid, tree-flatten, ack, range-prop, cumsum-xy), so the claim is 'faster on most', not all. The upto and reduce-update rows (0 ms vs 440/720 ms) reflect algorithmic differences (in-place updates, recursion handling) rather than constant-factor speed. The README's command line names gojq-0.12.17 while the table and footnote say 0.12.18. jq is a JSON filter-language interpreter, not one of the listed C++ baselines.

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; harness, filters and build profile are public. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 3.8k stars, 123 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-10-02 (active). Real category from an earlier wave: json (wave 4), since jaq is a jq clone and JSON query tool; language-interpreters also fits.

tier_reason: README (and README.en.md) tables compare every Wangshu tier with gopher-lua v1.1.2 run on the same runner in the same round; benchmark code is public (benchmarks/baseline, benchmarks/heavy, benchmarks/realworld, benchmarks/embedded, scripts/bench-readme-table.sh, .github/workflows/bench-readme-table.yml), the Go toolchain comes from go.mod (go 1.27.0 via setup-go go-version-file), go test flags are given, and CPUs are named for the Linux rows (Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, Azure Cobalt 100).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux/amd64 ratios over gopher-lua v1.1.2 (gopher time / Wangshu time): P4 method JIT in production 'auto' mode 18.0x HeavyArith, 17.7x HeavyFloatloop, 15.0x spectral-norm, 14.5x n-body, 9.35x fib, 7.51x fannkuch, 4.80x HeavyRecursion, 1.89x binary-trees; the non-production 'force' mode reaches 18.5x, 18.0x, 15.4x, 14.7x, 9.10x, 7.87x, 4.93x and 1.78x. The P1 interpreter is 1.27-5.54x faster on the micro, heavy and most small-program rows but slower on fib (0.87x) and fannkuch (0.77x). On the Go-to-Lua embedding rows Wangshu is slower than gopher-lua with the allocating Call API (CallOnly 0.41-0.47x, Boundary 0.56-0.64x, Predicate/Transform x1000 0.86-1.03x) and up to 1.52x faster only with the zero-alloc CallInto API. arm64 Cobalt 100 P4 peaks are 13.7x (HeavyArith) and 14.1x (HeavyFloatloop); macOS arm64 11.3x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (go.mod go directive, installed by actions/setup-go go-version-file); go test -run='^$' -bench=<tier pattern> -benchtime=2s -count=3 -cpu=1, median of 3; tiers selected by build tags (P1 default, P3/P4 tagged); script scripts/bench-readme-table.sh, workflow bench-readme-table (run 29098511106, 2026-07-10).
corrections.caveats: Baseline is gopher-lua (itself roughly 3x slower than C Lua per its own wiki), so the ratios say little about PUC Lua 5.x or LuaJIT; there is no PUC Lua timing in the table (Lua 5.1.5 is only the correctness oracle). Numbers come from shared GitHub-hosted runners; the README says wall times drift 10-20% between rounds, and the workflow header itself says hosted-runner numbers should not be pasted into the README, yet the README tables are those numbers. The headline peaks (18.5x etc.) are from the non-production 'force' mode; 'auto' is a little lower. P1 loses to gopher-lua on fib and fannkuch, and the embedding-boundary rows (the main use of an embeddable VM) are slower than gopher-lua with the Call API. P3 baseline columns run a different workload shape (kernel x50). macOS runner CPU named only as Apple M-series. New project with 8 stars.

notes: All quoted ratios appear on the page; record cherry-picked force-mode peaks and omitted that the Go-to-Lua Call boundary rows are slower than gopher-lua, corrected above. Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file), 8 stars, 1 fork, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-10-04 (active). Category language-interpreters fits; embedded-scripting (same wave) would also fit since it is an embeddable Lua 5.1 VM for Go.

tier_reason: docs/PERFORMANCE-CPYTHON-PARITY.md gives first-party per-fixture medians against CPython 3.14.8 from the project's own bench gate (crates/weavepy-bench, fixtures in crates/weavepy-bench/fixtures) on one Intel Core i9-9980HK laptop, but it does not state whether the WeavePy binary was the plain release or the PGO build, the Rust version (toolchain is unpinned 'stable'), or how CPython 3.14.8 was obtained or built (PR #83 description: not stated either). Partial methodology on own harness is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PERFORMANCE-CPYTHON-PARITY.md: geometric mean over 24 fixtures is 0.50 of CPython 3.14.8's time (about 2x faster, derived from page data) and 0.75 of main's; sumvm 0.05, jitloop and nested_loops 0.08, spectral_norm 0.20, fib 0.36, jitkernels 0.37, richards 0.55, pidigits 0.61, startup 0.79 of CPython's time; slower than CPython on deltablue (3.03x CPython's time) and generators (1.10x), dict_ops at parity (1.06; 0.92-1.06 across runs). PR #82 (2026-10-01) reported geomean 0.592 over 23 fixtures with a PGO build (tools/pgo_build.py). Imports of large stdlib packages still retire 1.3-1.8x CPython's instructions, and peak memory is up to 2-2.5x CPython's.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Release profile in Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, lto = fat, codegen-units 1); the parity doc says only 'release build', so whether tools/pgo_build.py (-Cprofile-generate/-Cprofile-use, trained on the benchmark fixtures at the harness work sizes plus regrtest and an import sweep) was used for the 0.50 run is not stated (PR #82's 0.592 run was PGO). Rust version not stated (rust-toolchain.toml pins 'stable'); CPython 3.14.8 source and build flags not stated. JIT on by default.
corrections.caveats: Own harness and fixtures on one development laptop (macOS x86-64, i9-9980HK); the CPython 3.14.8 build and its flags are not stated, and neither are the Rust version or whether the measured binary was PGO. The PGO script trains on the very benchmark fixtures at the exact work sizes used for timing, so PGO numbers are fixture-tuned. Fixture timers discard the computed result, so the harness does not check outputs (correctness rests on separate test suites). The README's per-wave history still lists committed baselines of 2.85x CPython's time (slower) on a macOS-aarch64 host, and the September PERFORMANCE.md showed process startup slower than CPython on ARM64 (32.27 ms vs 22.08 ms), so the 0.50 geomean is new (PR #83, 2026-10-05), from a different host, and not reproduced elsewhere; the A/B gates on Linux, macOS ARM64 and Windows compare against main, not CPython. The geomean is dominated by JIT-friendly loop kernels (sumvm, jitloop, nested_loops at 0.05-0.08). Peak memory up to 2-2.5x CPython's. Very new project: 80 commits, single author, 3 stars.

notes: Numbers are on the page and match PR #83; downgraded A to C because the run's build mode (PGO or not), Rust version and CPython provenance are unstated, PGO training uses the benchmark fixtures themselves, and earlier committed baselines in the README showed WeavePy 2.85x slower than CPython. Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0 and MIT license files (dual), 3 stars, 0 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-10-05 (active). 'Work-in-progress branch report' wording in the record is slightly off: the doc says 'This branch' but was merged into main via PR #83.
